L. Plaskota, G. W. Wasilkowski, Adaption allows efficient integration of functions with unknown singularities, Numer. Math. 102 (2005) 123-144
comparison.explanation: Adversary lower bound: every deterministic adaptive algorithm using n function values has error >= 2^-(n+1) on some f in J (one jump on a line, value on the surface arbitrary, constants 0 and 1 included), for the integral against the standard Gaussian measure. With R2 the minimal worst-case error is exactly 2^-(n+1). This is the integration counterpart of Sikorski's theorem that bisection is optimal for zero finding (optimal worst-case error (b-a)/2^(n+1)), transported to the Gaussian measure via the quantile transform (the Lean proofs hold for every atomless probability measure on R). It is consistent with Plaskota-Wasilkowski 2005 (one unknown singularity: adaption recovers the smooth rate); for piecewise-constant integrands the adaptive rate is exponential and we give the exact constant. A reproduction of classical bisection optimality, hence 'equal'.

Same optimal constant as Sikorski's bisection optimality for zero finding; within Plaskota-Wasilkowski's framework it is the piecewise-constant extreme (exponential rate). Equal to known results, with exact constants under the Gaussian measure.

comparison.explanation: Nonadaptive algorithms (n fixed nodes, arbitrary nonlinear output) have worst-case error >= 1/(2(n+1)) on J, and nodes at the Gaussian quantiles i/(n+1) attain it, so 1/(2(n+1)) is the exact minimal nonadaptive error, versus 2^-(n+1) adaptively (R1/R2): an exponential gap. Plaskota-Wasilkowski 2005 show that nonadaptive algorithms cannot converge faster than n^-1 for integrands with an unknown jump; Novak 1996 surveys when adaption helps (non-convex classes such as J). The value 1/(2(n+1)) coincides with Kiefer's optimal error for monotone functions (to which J essentially belongs after the quantile transform); we show the 0/1 step subclass is already extremal. Equal to known results.

comparison.explanation: Randomized lower bound on J: for any probability distribution over deterministic adaptive algorithms with n values (estimates measurable in the random parameter), some f in J has expected error >= 1/(2(2^(n+1)-1)) > 2^-(n+2), i.e. more than half the deterministic optimum 2^-(n+1) of R1/R2: randomization cannot improve bisection by a factor 2 or more. Proof by Bakhvalov's averaging technique (Novak 1988) over 2^(n+1) step functions: 0/1-valued information has at most 2^n outcomes. A standard technique and the classical order 2^-n; equal.
